faqs.question: How do you play Halloween charades?
faqs.answer: Split into two teams. One player draws a Halloween prompt and acts it out silently for 60 seconds while their own team guesses; no speaking, mouthing, spelling or pointing at objects. Score 2 points for a correct guess inside 30 seconds and 1 point inside 60, and let the other team try one steal on a miss.

faqs.question: What are good Halloween charades ideas for kids?
faqs.answer: For ages 4 to 7, use single creatures or actions they can become: werewolf, zombie, wizard, dragon, robot, knocking on a door or putting on a mask. For ages 8 to 12, add a twist, such as a zombie learning to dance or a robot running out of battery.

faqs.question: What are hard Halloween charades for adults?
faqs.answer: Situation phrases are hardest because the team must guess every word, for example "a witch failing her flying test" or "eating soup through a full-face mask". Old book titles such as The Fall of the House of Usher (1839) are also tough, since the actor has to signal a seven-word title.

faqs.question: How long should each turn be in charades?
faqs.answer: 60 seconds is the common limit and keeps a group of 12 to about 18 minutes per round, allowing 30 seconds to swap actors. Young children can have 90 seconds, and the dumb crambo variant works on the same 60-second clock.

faqs.question: What are the hand signals in charades?
faqs.answer: Fingers held up give the number of words; fingers laid on the forearm give the number of syllables; tugging an earlobe means "sounds like"; finger and thumb almost touching means a short word such as "the"; and touching your nose while pointing at someone means they are right. Agree on the set before playing, because house rules differ.

faqs.question: What is reverse charades?
faqs.answer: In reverse charades the whole team acts and only one player guesses. A Halloween version uses frozen tableaux: lights off while the team poses, on for 5 seconds, with up to 3 tableaux inside 60 seconds.

faqs.question: Where did the game of charades come from?
faqs.answer: The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the charade as a syllable riddle probably invented in France in the 18th century. Acted charades were fashionable in England by the 1840s; Thackeray's Vanity Fair (1847–48) says they had come over from France.

faqs.question: Can I use horror film titles in Halloween charades?
faqs.answer: You can, but only if everyone playing has seen the films, which rarely holds across ages. Book titles from 1818 to 1902, such as Frankenstein, Dracula and The Invisible Man, are widely known, long out of copyright and never go out of date.

faqs.question: Should sound effects be allowed in charades?
faqs.answer: Allow them for children under 8 and ban them for everyone else. In a 2026 study of 71 pairs, gesture alone was guessed about 45% of the time and gesture plus sounds about 46%, so sounds barely help adults.

faqs.question: How many people do you need for Halloween charades?
faqs.answer: Six to 16 is the comfortable range for two teams. With fewer than 6, play cooperatively and count how many prompts the group gets in 10 minutes; above 16, split into two games or switch to reverse charades.

faqs.question: Can SubhSandesh run a Halloween charades game?
faqs.answer: No. SubhSandesh's Halloween pages are greeting pages for one person, not party tools, so they cannot hand out prompts or keep score. They suit a friend who missed the game: the interactive card holds up to six photos, and the premium page adds a voice note up to 60 seconds.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Charades: 55 Original Prompts, Rules and Scoring

Halloween charades is the classic silent acting game with an October deck: one player mimes a creature, an action or a story title for 60 seconds while their team calls out guesses. Below are 55 original prompts by age (4–7, 8–12, teens and adults, plus 10 public-domain book titles), the standard hand signals, a points system and a reverse version.

Each list fits on one phone screen. On SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone (27,725 of 57,456 views) and each page averages 11.1 views, so the actor can glance at a list, pocket it and check it again next turn. Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027.

## What is Halloween charades, and where did charades come from?

Halloween charades is ordinary charades with a spooky prompt set: the actor may not speak, spell or mouth words, and the team must name the exact prompt before time runs out. The parent game dates back to 18th-century France.

The [1911 Encyclopædia Britannica entry on the charade](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Charade) calls it a riddle "probably invented in France during the 18th century", in which each syllable is described as a word of its own. By 1911 the acted version, syllable by syllable on a stage, was the most popular form.

In chapter 51 of Thackeray's *Vanity Fair* (serialised 1847–48), the narrator says "the amiable amusement of acting charades had come among us from France", and a hidden manager calls "First two syllables" between costumed scenes that build up to AGAMEMNON ([Project Gutenberg text](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/599)). Those scenes still had spoken lines, so the fully silent rule is a later habit.

The "sounds like" signal has an ancestor too. Britannica's [1911 entry on crambo](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Crambo) describes Dumb Crambo, in which players get a rhyme and must express the hidden word "by dumb show".

## 55 original Halloween charades ideas, by age

Each set moves up a step, from one thing to a scene to a full situation. The last set uses books from 1818 to 1902 instead of films, so nobody needs to have seen a particular one.

### 1. Ages 4–7: 15 single creatures and actions

Whisper the prompt or show a picture to pre-readers. Allow growls at this age only; for a 5-year-old the noise is half the fun.

- Werewolf
- Zombie
- Wizard
- Pirate
- Dragon
- Robot
- Fairy
- Knocking on a door
- Ringing a doorbell
- Putting on a mask
- Tiptoeing in the dark
- Hiding under a blanket
- Unwrapping a sweet
- Getting your face painted
- Howling at night

### 2. Ages 8–12: 15 short scenes

Each scene needs two moves: act the character first, then what they are doing.

- A zombie learning to dance
- A werewolf getting a haircut
- A wizard whose wand won't work
- A robot running out of battery
- A dragon with a terrible sneeze
- A fairy with a bent wing
- A pirate digging for treasure at night
- Sorting your trick-or-treat haul
- Trading sweets with a friend
- Hiding the biggest chocolate bar
- Getting stuck in a costume zip
- Walking through a corn maze
- Carving a jack-o'-lantern with a spoon
- Reading a scary story under the covers
- Getting spooked by your own shadow

### 3. Teens and adults: 15 situation phrases

The team must say the whole phrase, so use the word-count and "sounds like" signals. All 15 are clean for a mixed family party.

- A werewolf hiding in a yoga class
- A witch failing her flying test
- A vampire at a garlic-bread tasting
- A zombie waiting for a delayed bus
- A ghost hunter whose torch keeps dying
- Losing your group in a haunted maze
- Handing out the last sweet to forty children
- Eating soup through a full-face mask
- A mad scientist's experiment working for once
- Getting your cape caught in a lift door
- Dancing at a party on stilts
- A toddler refusing to take off a dinosaur suit
- Explaining Halloween to a confused grandparent
- A jack-o'-lantern that keeps collapsing
- Posing for a group photo with a werewolf

### 4. Public-domain story titles: 10 books from 1818 to 1902

Signal "book" with open palms, then the word count. Every book here is long out of copyright.

- *Frankenstein* (Mary Shelley, 1818): stomp stiff-legged
- *The Legend of Sleepy Hollow* (Washington Irving, 1820)
- *The Fall of the House of Usher* (Edgar Allan Poe, 1839): a roof caving in
- *The Tell-Tale Heart* (Poe, 1843): thump a heartbeat
- *The Raven* (Poe, 1845): flap and tilt your head
- *Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde* (Robert Louis Stevenson, 1886): drink, then transform
- *The Canterville Ghost* (Oscar Wilde, 1887): rattle invisible chains
- *Dracula* (Bram Stoker, 1897): a cape across your face
- *The Invisible Man* (H. G. Wells, 1897): unwind bandages from an empty head
- *The Hound of the Baskervilles* (Arthur Conan Doyle, 1902)

## Halloween charades rules: signals, 60-second turns and scoring

Play 2 teams of 3 to 8; the other team picks each prompt and the actor gets 60 seconds. No speaking, mouthing, finger-spelling or pointing at things, and costumes count as things, so nobody points at a guest dressed as the answer.

Most groups use these 8 signals. Agree on them first, because house versions differ.

- **Number of words:** hold up that many fingers, then fingers again for the word you are acting.
- **Number of syllables:** lay that many fingers on your forearm.
- **Sounds like:** tug your earlobe, then act a rhyming word.
- **Short word ("a", "of", "the"):** hold finger and thumb almost touching.
- **Book title:** open your palms side by side.
- **The whole thing:** sweep both arms in a wide circle.
- **Close, keep going:** beckon with both hands.
- **Correct:** touch your nose and point at the guesser.

Score 2 points for a guess inside 30 seconds and 1 point inside 60; on a miss, the other team gets one shout to steal the point. Allowing 30 seconds to swap actors, 12 players need about 18 minutes per round.

## How well do people guess silent gestures? What two studies found

In a [2026 study in *Behavior Research Methods*](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13263253), Aleksandra Ćwiek, Susanne Fuchs, Wim Pouw and Šárka Kadavá had 71 pairs of young adults communicate 84 concepts without words: gesture alone was guessed correctly about 45% of the time, gesture plus sounds about 46%, and sounds alone about 12%.

So banning sound effects for teens and adults costs almost nothing, and with only about 32% of attempts landing overall, the steal rule keeps hard rounds moving. Players' own ratings of how easy a concept was to express predicted success, so cut any prompt you cannot picture acting.

How you act matters too. In a [2020 database of silent gestures](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7005091), Gerardo Ortega and Aslı Özyürek asked 20 Dutch adults to mime 109 concepts, who passed on only 8% of trials (444 of 5,440). Actions and handheld objects were shown by miming their use, things too big to hold were traced in the air, and animate beings were shown by becoming them.

So become the werewolf, mime the spoon carving, and trace the maze walls. A [2021 paper by Piotr Żywiczyński, Sławomir Wacewicz and Casey Lister](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8059511) names charades as a game where pantomime returns because language is blocked, and notes the actor usually stands, freeing the whole body.

## Reverse charades and one older Halloween variant

Both reuse the prompt lists above with the same 60-second clock. What changes is who acts and who guesses.

### Tableau reverse charades

The whole team acts and one player guesses, using frozen Victorian-style scenes. Lights off while the team poses, on for 5 seconds, up to 3 tableaux inside 60 seconds; it suits the book titles and gives a shy guest a role with no spotlight.

### Dumb crambo round

Guessers hear only a clue such as "it rhymes with fright", then act their guesses instead of saying them while the clue-giver nods or shakes their head. One-syllable words with easy rhymes work best: fright, howl, creep, chill.

The three formats compared (editorial guidance, not measured data):

| Format | Players | Turn length | Prep | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Classic team charades | 6–16 | 60 s | 10 min to cut slips | Ages 6 and up, mixed families |
| Tableau reverse charades | 8–20 | 60 s, 3 tableaux | 2 min, one light switch | Large groups, shy guests |
| Dumb crambo round | 4–10 | 60 s | 5 min to pick rhymes | Word lovers aged 10 and up |

Switch from classic to tableaux once the group passes about 16 people.

## A Halloween page for the one person who missed the game

SubhSandesh will not run charades, keep score or invite guests; it is not a party tool. Its two Halloween templates are greeting pages for one person (partner, bestie, family or kids mode), which suits the friend who was ill or abroad on the night.

[The interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes, holds up to six photos from the night, and lets you choose the word carved on its jack-o'-lantern, so make it the prompt your team never guessed. [The premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about 10 minutes and adds a voice note up to 60 seconds, up to 12 photos and a reply box for one answer of up to 280 characters.

For an in-joke, add a password, as 38.5% of SubhSandesh creators do (2,000 of 5,199). For someone who skips Halloween entirely, [the full SubhSandesh template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) has birthday and love pages.

## When charades is the wrong Halloween game

- **Under-4s.** Keeping a prompt secret is hard at this age; a follow-the-leader monster walk works better.
- **Players who cannot stand.** Seated actors do best with the 8–12 scenes, which read from the waist up.
- **More than 16 people.** One round runs past 25 minutes; split into two games or switch to tableaux.
- **Thanking every guest.** Each Halloween page is addressed to one recipient with English-only screens; a group chat message reaches 12 people faster.

## Sources

- Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), "Charade" and "Crambo", via Wikisource.
- W. M. Thackeray, *Vanity Fair*, chapter 51 (1847–48), Project Gutenberg.
- Ćwiek, Fuchs, Pouw and Kadavá (2026), *Behavior Research Methods*, 12 June 2026.
- Ortega and Özyürek (2020), *Behavior Research Methods*, February 2020.
- Żywiczyński, Wacewicz and Lister (2021), *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B*, 22 March 2021.

auditReport.honestAssessment: The ranking pages (icebreakerideas, getcharadesideas, charades-generator, 101planners, paperheartfamily) are uncited word lists built around film titles; none gives the game's history, a scoring rule tied to a timer, or any evidence on how well silent gestures are guessed. This post adds 55 original film-free prompts, a primary-sourced origin and three open-access gesture papers, which are citable claims those pages lack. It cannot match their prompt counts (95–100+) or their printable cards, and the domain authority gap means ranking, if it comes, will take months.

structuralLimitations: No Halloween usage data in facts.md; first-party facts are platform-wide.

Brief said parlour charades are '18th–19th c.': verified with nuance — the written syllable riddle is 18th-century France (Britannica 1911, 'probably'); acted charades are documented in England by 1847–48 (Vanity Fair) and still used spoken lines, so the fully silent mime form is later. No primary source found for when the modern hand signals were standardised; they are presented as common convention, not dated.
